name: Orlistat
route_note: oral capsule with each main meal containing fat (120 mg prescription; 60 mg OTC)

discovery.note: A hydrogenated derivative of lipstatin, a natural lipase inhibitor produced by Streptomyces toxytricini.

rx_status: prescription (120 mg); OTC in many countries (60 mg)
tagline: A weight-loss pill that blocks fat digestion in the gut
summary: Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases in the gut so that about 30% of dietary fat passes unabsorbed. It produces modest weight loss alongside a reduced-calorie diet and is available over the counter at a lower dose in many countries; oily stools and faecal urgency are common.
mechanism: Orlistat forms a covalent bond with the active-site serine of gastric and pancreatic lipases in the stomach and small-intestinal lumen. The inactivated enzymes cannot hydrolyse dietary triglycerides into absorbable free fatty acids and monoglycerides.
Undigested fat is excreted in the faeces, reducing calorie absorption. Systemic absorption is minimal, so effects are largely confined to the gut; absorption of fat-soluble vitamins can also fall.
uses: Obesity (BMI ≥30) or overweight (BMI ≥27) with risk factors, with a reduced-calorie diet
Reducing risk of weight regain after prior weight loss

history.title: EU approval
history.detail: Xenical is approved in the European Union.

history.title: XENDOS
history.detail: The four-year XENDOS study reports a 37% reduction in type 2 diabetes incidence with orlistat plus lifestyle change.

history.title: OTC alli
history.detail: FDA approves 60 mg orlistat (alli) as the first OTC weight-loss drug in the US; EU OTC approval follows in 2009.

history.title: Liver injury labelling
history.detail: FDA adds information about rare reports of severe liver injury to orlistat labels.

pk.metabolism: mainly in the gut wall to inactive metabolites

serious: reduced absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, ciclosporin and levothyroxine

facts: Orlistat derives from lipstatin, a natural product of the soil bacterium Streptomyces toxytricini.
alli became the first FDA-approved over-the-counter weight-loss drug in 2007.
